mioc-036.title: Arabia slams into Eurasia and the Tethys narrows
mioc-036.text: In the Early Miocene the Arabian part of Africa collided with Eurasia, cutting the Mediterranean off from the Indian Ocean. The first step of the closure, about 20 million years ago, cut water exchange by 90%. Two forces worked together. Africa-Arabia moved north, and sea level fell as the Antarctic Ice Sheet grew. By the mid-Burdigalian the collision had built a land bridge joining the two landmasses. The dates are contested. Sources place the Tethys closure anywhere from about 35 to 19-12 million years ago. The two-step story used here, ending in {{ref:mioc-082}}, is one reading.

mioc-042.title: Most open-ocean sharks vanish
mioc-042.text: About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared. Seven in ten kinds of shark that roamed the high seas were simply gone. The ocean did not stay empty for long. The seas that followed came to be ruled by large predators such as megalodon, met in {{ref:mioc-027}}, and the giant sperm whale Livyatan. The gap left by the lost sharks was filled by some of the biggest hunters the oceans have known.

mioc-053.title: The Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum
mioc-053.text: Around 15 million years ago, during the warmest part of the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, global temperature averaged about 18.4 °C, and the Antarctic ice cap shrank. Between roughly 17 and 14 million years ago, the climate was about 3 °C warmer than today. Foraminifera, tiny shelled organisms living on the seafloor, keep the timetable in their shells. They put the onset at 16.9 Ma, the peak at 15.3 Ma and the end at 13.8 Ma. A positive shift in carbon isotopes, the Monterey Carbon Excursion, began just before the warmth and ended just after it. The cause is debated. The Columbia River flood basalts in {{ref:mioc-054}}, helped by volcanic gas at plate margins, are seen as the main driver. Yet the warming began about 16.9 Ma, and the basalts cannot explain warming before 16.3 Ma. Something else must have started it, and researchers still disagree on what.

mioc-055.title: Steens Mountain catches the magnetic field flipping
mioc-055.text: Lava flows at Steens Mountain in Oregon froze a record of Earth's magnetic field as it reversed, about 16.7 Ma. They suggest the field can shift up to 6 degrees a day, astonishingly fast. The reversal that ended the magnetic period called Chron C5Cr was not one clean flip but a series of reversals and excursions.

mioc-054.title: The Columbia River basalts flood the Northwest
mioc-054.text: Lava buried a whole region in a geological instant. Between 16.7 and 15.9 Ma, the Columbia River flood basalts poured out 95% of all their lava over the Columbia Plateau and Oregon. This large igneous province, linked to the Yellowstone hotspot, totals about 210,000 cubic km of rock. Its Roza Member alone held at least 1,500 cubic km. A mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock, is the most widely accepted cause, though the question is still debated. The eruptions reshaped the volcanic life of the region. They ended the Western Cascades period, and Cascade volcanism stayed at a low point from 17 to 9 Ma. They are often blamed for the warming in {{ref:mioc-053}}. That link is disputed, because the warming began earlier, around 16.9 Ma, before the main pulse of lava.

mioc-056.title: The Yellowstone hotspot's first calderas
mioc-056.text: The Yellowstone hotspot is thought to have arrived under North America in the Miocene, and it is still active. Its first calderas formed 16.5 to 15.5 million years ago, among them McDermitt and Virgin Valley, as the Steens flood basalts waned. McDermitt Caldera formed about 16.4 million years ago when a rhyolite lava dome collapsed. Eruptions such as the Longridge Caldera's, 15.6 million years ago, produced up to 400 cubic km of tuff. The hotspot's later track is told in {{ref:mioc-096}}.

mioc-058.title: Clarkia's leaves still blush with autumn color
mioc-058.text: Some leaves from Idaho's Clarkia beds still show autumn colors when first exposed, then fade as air oxidizes them. Small amounts of ancient DNA have reportedly been isolated from them. The beds lie within the Wanapum Basalts of the Columbia River lavas, dated 16.1 to 15.9 million years ago.

mioc-059.title: The hippopotamus lineage begins
mioc-059.text: The hippopotamus evolved around 16 million years ago, in the middle of the Miocene. Its family took shape during the warm stretch of the epoch, alongside the many other mammal groups that appeared or diversified then, from mastodons and bovids to kangaroos.

mioc-060.title: McGraths Flat keeps microscopic soft tissue
mioc-060.text: Soft tissue almost never fossilizes, and in Australia it is especially rare. At McGraths Flat in New South Wales, unusual conditions preserved microscopic soft-tissue detail. The site has revealed invertebrate species no one had known before.

mioc-062.title: Australia begins to collide with Southeast Asia
mioc-062.text: Australia had been drifting north since it broke from Antarctica. In the Middle Miocene, it began to collide with Southeast Asia. The collision did more than crumple crust. It blocked the equatorial ocean flow between the western Pacific and the Indian Ocean, closing a warm-water passage along the equator.

mioc-063.title: The last creodonts disappear
mioc-063.text: The last creodonts, early predatory mammals, died out in the Middle Miocene. They had already retreated to Africa and the Middle East, as {{ref:olig-076}} describes. Carnivorans now had the predator roles to themselves.

mioc-064.title: Most modern seed plants appear
mioc-064.text: Many new plants evolved in the mid-Miocene, including 95% of modern seed plants. Most of the plant kinds growing today, in other words, trace their origin to this one stretch of time.

mioc-065.title: The Badenian Flooding refreshes the Paratethys
mioc-065.text: About 15 Ma the sea rose across a wide area, an event called the Badenian Flooding. It reconnected the Paratethys with the global ocean. Fresh ocean water flowed in and ventilated its deep basins, ending the long oxygen starvation described in {{ref:olig-015}}. The sea came alive. It held a tropical to subtropical ecosystem with coral reefs and high biodiversity, and many of its species lived nowhere else.

mioc-066.title: First mastodons, bovids and kangaroos
mioc-066.text: Around 15 million years ago, three famous groups made their first appearance: mastodons of the genus Mammut, bovids such as cattle and antelopes, and kangaroos. Australian megafauna, the continent's large animals, diversified at the same time.

mioc-067.title: Earth's magnetic field flips again and again
mioc-067.text: Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times, but around 15 million years ago it was especially restless. At least 51 reversals occurred in a 12-million-year period centred on that date. Each one is written into rocks that cooled while it lasted.

mioc-068.title: Lake Vostok is sealed beneath the ice
mioc-068.text: Beneath the East Antarctic ice lies a lake, Lake Vostok. Its water is estimated to have been sealed under the thick ice about 15 million years ago, when the ice sheet formed over it. It has stayed cut off from the open air ever since.

mioc-071.title: Steinheim, the Ries crater's small neighbor
mioc-071.text: About 40 km southwest of the Ries lies a smaller crater, Steinheim, 3.8 km across and also roughly 15 million years old. The two were long thought to come from one binary asteroid. That is now disputed. A 2020 study suggests Steinheim is about 500,000 years younger.

mioc-070.title: The Pisco Formation's marine treasures
mioc-070.text: Peru's Pisco Formation ranks among the most important Lagerstätten, fossil sites of exceptional preservation. It holds megalodon, penguins, whales, marine crocodiles and aquatic sloths, a crowded record of coastal sea life.

mioc-072.title: An asteroid blasts the Ries crater in Germany
mioc-072.text: The blast that hit southern Germany 14.808 ± 0.038 million years ago released about 2.4×10^21 joules, the power of 40 million Hiroshima bombs. An asteroid had struck, carving the 24 km Nördlinger Ries crater. Melted surface sand flew up to 450 km away. It is thought to be the source of moldavites, green glassy tektites found in the Czech Republic. A smaller crater nearby may or may not be linked, as {{ref:mioc-071}} explains.

mioc-074.title: Cooling ends the warm Miocene's tropical Europe
mioc-074.text: During the warm optimum, central Europe held monitor lizards, chameleons, cordylid lizards, alligators and giant turtles. Then a wave of extinctions on land and at sea, the Middle Miocene disruption, followed about 14.8 to 14.5 Ma. The crocodilians Gavialosuchus and Diplocynodon vanished from northern latitudes between 14 and 13.5 Ma. Cooling wiped out the coral reefs of the Paratethys. Desmostylians began a decline they would not recover from.

mioc-073.title: The great Middle Miocene cooling
mioc-073.text: Antarctic summers cooled by at least 8 °C. Around 13.94 Ma, annual temperatures in the Transantarctic Mountains fell 25–30 °C, and their glaciers froze to their beds. This was the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, a major and permanent cooling step between 14.8 and 14.1 Ma that ended the warm optimum. Cold Antarctic deep water increased. The East Antarctic Ice Sheet expanded, reaching roughly its present size by 14 Ma. The rocks carry a signal of the change in Earth's orbit. A flip in the 41,000-year obliquity cycle, the slow nodding of Earth's tilt, around 14.0–13.8 Ma is read as a sign of the ice expansion. The cold reached the deep sea too. The resulting change in ocean circulation is thought to have caused the Miocene Carbonate Crash in the early Tortonian. From here, the Miocene world turns steadily colder and drier.

mioc-076.title: The Chile Triple Junction forms
mioc-076.text: About 14 million years ago, the Antarctic Plate began sliding beneath South America. The Chile Ridge, a spreading ridge, collided with the continent near Tierra del Fuego. Where the three plates meet, the Chile Triple Junction formed.

mioc-077.title: Paleolake Boreas, a tundra lake in Antarctica
mioc-077.text: Around 14 million years ago, a lake in Antarctica sat in tundra conditions, cold but not yet fully icebound. Its sediments preserved ostracods, tiny shelled crustaceans, right down to their soft anatomy.

mioc-079.title: The Sea of Japan opens at both ends
mioc-079.text: By 14 million years ago, the Sea of Japan basin was open to the northeast and southwest. Rising seas isolated Japan further from the mainland, continuing the opening that began in {{ref:olig-069}}.

mioc-078.title: The Andes cast a rain shadow over Patagonia
mioc-078.text: Mountains can make deserts. As the southern Andes rose 14 to 12 million years ago, they blocked moist air and cast a rain shadow, a dry zone downwind of a range. East of the mountains, the Patagonian Desert formed.

mioc-080.title: Tibet nears its modern height
mioc-080.text: India kept pushing into Asia through the Neogene, building the Himalayas, and the Tibetan Plateau climbed with them. East–west rift valleys in the Lhasa and Himalaya terranes suggest the plateau was close to its modern altitude by about 14 to 8 Ma. Sudden mafic volcanism and faster uplift 14 to 11 Ma point to delamination, the peeling away of the dense lower lithosphere beneath Tibet. Accounts differ, however. The plateau may have neared its present height by the late Oligocene, yet some suture zones stayed tropical lowlands into the early Miocene. Its rise affected the Asian monsoons.

mioc-082.title: The Tethys seaway closes for good
mioc-082.text: The second and final step of the Tethys seaway's closure came around 13.8 Ma, as Antarctic glaciers expanded sharply. A link between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean had briefly reopened in the Langhian, then closed for good. Africa collided with Eurasia in the Turkish–Arabian region, and the old seaway disappeared. The timing is contested. Sources date the closure anywhere from about 50 or 35 Ma to 19-12 Ma, and this two-step account, begun in {{ref:mioc-036}}, follows only some of them.

mioc-081.title: The Badenian Salinity Crisis
mioc-081.text: Midway through the Middle Miocene, rising central European mountains and falling sea level cut the Paratethys off from the ocean. Around 13.8 Ma the Bârlad Strait closed, and the Eastern Paratethys became a saltwater lake. Starved of fresh water, the Central Paratethys laid down evaporites, salt left by evaporating water, until about 13.4 Ma. Growing isolation wiped out most small and mid-sized deepwater and open-ocean sharks there. The crisis was a smaller rehearsal of the Mediterranean's own drying in {{ref:mioc-154}}.

mioc-083.title: La Venta's tropical menagerie
mioc-083.text: La Venta in Colombia holds a rich tropical fauna, with glyptodonts, notoungulates and ground sloths, that lived about 13.8 to 12 million years ago. The site names the Laventan age, the only South American land-mammal age defined north of the equator.

mioc-084.title: Ōkueyama's supereruption in Japan
mioc-084.text: About 13.7 million years ago, Mount Ōkueyama in Japan erupted massively, possibly at VEI 8. That would make it larger than any eruption in recorded history. It was one of several huge eruptions across southwest Japan between 15 and 13 million years ago.

mioc-086.title: Fish suffocate in Ngorora's lakes
mioc-086.text: In Kenya's Ngorora beds, alkaline lake sediments hold whole fish skeletons, still joined, that died en masse. They suffocated, either during ash falls or when the lake water turned acidic quickly. Each layer marks a sudden die-off.

mioc-089.title: The Paratethys turns brackish and its sea life dies
mioc-089.text: From 13.36 to 12.65 Ma, the Central Paratethys was open sea again. Then the Bârlad Strait reopened, and the sea turned brackish, between salt and fresh. That change caused the Badenian–Sarmatian extinction event.

mioc-090.title: The Qaidam Basin dries out
mioc-090.text: Around 12.6 Ma, the weathering of silicate rock in China's Qaidam Basin fell sharply. Weathering needs water, so the drop marks a major aridification event, the basin turning dry.

mioc-091.title: Sivapithecus, the ape with an orangutan's face
mioc-091.text: Sivapithecus, a chimpanzee-sized ape, lived in the Indian subcontinent about 12.5-8.5 million years ago. Its face resembled an orangutan's, with a concave profile, large cheekbones and close-set eyes. A skull from Pakistan strengthened the link. One species may have been the orangutans' ancestor.

mioc-092.title: Ashfall: a waterhole buried by a distant eruption
mioc-092.text: One rhino at Nebraska's Ashfall Fossil Beds still carries an unborn fetus. Ash from the Bruneau-Jarbidge supereruption in Idaho drifted about 1,600 km east and buried a waterhole. Teleoceras rhinos, horses, camels and birds lie articulated. They died of lung failure from inhaled ash.

mioc-093.title: Bullock Creek's skulls and horned tortoise
mioc-093.text: Bullock Creek in Australia's Northern Territory preserves complete marsupial skulls, the crocodile Baru, an early kangaroo and the horned tortoise Meiolania. Whole skulls are rare finds, and here they give a clear view of the animals of Miocene northern Australia.

mioc-095.title: The Eridanos, a lost river, builds a giant delta
mioc-095.text: A great river once flowed from Lapland across the Baltic region. By about 12 Ma at the latest, this Eridanos had reached the North Sea area. Its sediments built an immense delta, reckoned comparable in size to the modern Amazon's.

mioc-097.title: The Paratethys becomes a brackish megalake
mioc-097.text: Around 12 Ma, the Paratethys became a megalake of over 2.8 million km², reaching from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan. It was the size of an inland sea but no longer part of the ocean. Its water was brackish, with salinity mostly 12–14‰, far fresher than seawater. Trapped by tectonics and cut off from the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, it became an isolated inland sea that gradually disappeared. Its final crisis is told in {{ref:mioc-161}}.

mioc-098.title: Pliohippus and the rise of the grazing horses
mioc-098.text: Around 10 Ma, horses grew larger and developed high-crowned teeth built for grinding tough grass. The family tree behind them branched from Merychippus, the ancestor of Hipparion, Protohippus and Pliohippus. Pliohippus itself arose from Calippus around 12 Ma. Hipparion and its relatives multiplied in North America. At least one of them migrated to Asia and Europe, carrying the grazing horse lineage across the northern continents.

mioc-096.title: Supereruptions build the Snake River Plain
mioc-096.text: Two of the eruptions here rank as VEI 8 supereruptions. McMullen, 8.99 Ma, released at least 1,700 km³ of rock, and Grey's Landing, 8.72 Ma, at least 2,800 km³. They belong to a chain. The western Snake River Plain began forming around 12–11 Ma with rhyolite lava and ignimbrite. The Yellowstone hotspot's Picabo caldera erupted the Arbon Valley Tuff about 10.2 Ma, and the Twin Falls field was active 10–8.6 Ma. From 6.6 Ma the Heise field in eastern Idaho produced four big caldera eruptions, starting with 1,500 km³ of Blacktail Tuff at 6.62 Ma. Volcanism marched both ways. Oregon's High Lava Plains spread west from about 10 Ma while the Snake River Plain advanced east.

mioc-094.title: The deep seaway between the Americas closes
mioc-094.text: By 12–9.2 Ma, the deep-ocean links between the Pacific and the Caribbean through Central America had closed. A shallow link lasted until 2.45 Ma at the latest. The first phase of uplift of the Isthmus of Panama is dated to around 12 Ma. In the Late Miocene islands formed between the continents, and ground sloths such as Thinobadistes island-hopped north. Zircons in northern Colombia suggest a full isthmus, not just islands, may already have formed by 10 Ma. Colombia's La Venta fauna is the last purely South American assemblage before the two continents' animals mixed.

mioc-099.title: The Amazon runs across a continent
mioc-099.text: In the Cretaceous, the proto-Amazon flowed west, part of a river system draining from Africa. The river we know flows the other way. Between 11.8 and 11.3 Ma, the Amazon began flowing as a river across the whole continent. Its new course ran through the region once held by the wetland in {{ref:mioc-032}}.

reviews.miocene-epoch: The Miocene was a long slide from warmth into cold, with one great warm spell in the middle. Rising mountains drove much of it: the Andes and Tibet climbed, their rain shadows and monsoons dried the land, and grasses spread until grazing horses outnumbered browsers. A land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia closed the Tethys and let apes, elephants and many other animals cross. Flood basalts on the Columbia Plateau came with the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, and a sharp cooling step afterward grew the East Antarctic Ice Sheet to roughly its present size. In the shrinking Paratethys and the newly joined Americas, the same story played out: changing seaways set the fate of the life within them.
